title: Chain and text
hook: every hadith has a chain of narrators and a text

segments.voice: Yesterday, sunnah and hadith: the way, and the reports that carry it. Your line was the way, carried. Which small sunnah did you try? Day one thousand one hundred forty-five.

Al-Humaydi told us. Sufyan told us. Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari told us. That's not a cast list. It's how the first report in Sahih al-Bukhari begins, put into plain English. Before the reader reaches a single word the Prophet said, there's a line of people, each handing the words to the next. The words themselves come later, and we met them on this path once already: actions are judged by intentions. Today we stay with the part that's easy to skim. The names. Today, the isnad.
screen: `AL-HUMAYDI TOLD US.` → `BEFORE THE WORDS, THE NAMES.` → `THE PART THAT'S EASY TO SKIM.`

segments.voice: First, two parts. A hadith, as the scholars lay it out, has a chain and a text. The chain is the isnad: who told whom. The text is the matn: what was said. Tomorrow is the text. Today is the chain. Second, walk it. After Yahya ibn Sa'id, the chain in Bukhari goes on: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi told him that he heard Alqamah ibn Waqqas say: I heard Umar ibn al-Khattab on the pulpit say: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say. Read in order, it's a road back. From al-Bukhari's own teacher, hand to hand, back to Umar standing on a pulpit, and from him to the Prophet. Third, listen to the verbs. Told us. Told me. I heard. Scholars of hadith paid close attention to those small words, because they can show how each person received the report: in a gathering, alone, face to face. A vaguer word, a plain "from so-and-so", could leave room for a question. Did these two actually meet? Fourth, what the chain is for. Once the names are written down, every one of them can be checked. Was he honest? Was his memory careful? Did he live in the same place and time as the man he quotes? A beautiful saying with a gap in its chain, or with a name nobody can vouch for, is held back. Sunni collections build their chains through the companions. Shia collections build theirs too, often running through the Imams of the Prophet's family. Different roads, one habit: before you accept the words, you ask who carried them, one link at a time.
screen: `A CHAIN, AND A TEXT.` · `WALK IT BACK TO THE PULPIT.` · `TOLD US. TOLD ME. I HEARD.` · `EVERY NAME CAN BE CHECKED.`

segments.voice: The practice: trace one chain. Settle, and breathe. Choose one piece of news you heard this week about someone you know. A job, an illness, a rumor. Now build its isnad, out loud in your head, the way the collections do. Who told me? And who told them? And where did that person get it? Say it in the old form if it helps: so-and-so told me, that so-and-so told her. Go back as far as you honestly can. Then find the link where the chain goes quiet, the place where you have to say: I don't know who told them. Rest there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Isnad. The chain of narrators at the head of a hadith: who told whom, link by link, back to the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: who told whom. Today, when you pass on any news, say where you got it. Tomorrow: the text itself. Day one thousand one hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: In hadith collections each report is printed with its chain of narrators before its text, and students of hadith learn to read the chain, check each narrator and notice the words of transmission.

fork.setup: you're a hadith scholar. a lovely saying reaches you, but one name in its chain is a man no one can vouch for. what do you do?
options: accept it; the words are beautiful.
hold it back until the link can be checked.
replace the name with a better one.
fork.reveal: a gap or an unknown name in the chain holds a report back, however lovely its words.

original.note: the chain of narrators at the head of a hadith.

trapdoor: what you thought: the names at the start of a hadith are a formality.
what it means: the isnad is the chain of who told whom, and every name in it can be checked.
what a scholar hears: 'told us', 'told me', 'I heard', 'from': the words of transmission themselves show how each link received the report.

notes: Chain of Bukhari 1 given from memory: confirm names and order, and that Umar was on the pulpit (minbar) in this narration.
Statements on words of transmission (haddathana, akhbarana, sami'tu, 'an) and their significance are general hadith-science points, not in the cited text; confirm wording.
Shia chains 'often running through the Imams': confirm phrasing is fair.
Day 1060 used Ibn al-Mubarak's saying and the ijaza; this day avoids both. Day 930 used Bukhari 1's text as its hook; here the focus is its chain.
